source_excerpts.text:
I selected the gap between rank-one stability and stability under arbitrary compatible deformations. The most substantial result of this investigation is an exact obstruction theorem for the Burkholder family: a pointwise positive correction exists, but every possible closed two-form correction of the specified local type is impossible.
This rules out an entire proof mechanism, not merely a particular ansatz. The constructive continuation is a different, finite-dimensional problem for arbitrary planar homogeneous quartics, with a precisely defined determinant-removal operation and an explicit remaining existence statement.
The arguments below are complete for the stated intermediate results. Their historical novelty and independent correctness remain unverified. The positive quartic existence statement is not proved.
For an energy density \(F:\mathbb R^{2\times2}\to\mathbb R\), rank-one convexity means
\[ D^2F(A)[\eta\otimes\xi,\eta\otimes\xi]\geq0 \]
for every matrix \(A\) and vectors \(\eta,\xi\).
Quasiconvexity asks for the much stronger conclusion
\[ \int_U F(A+D\varphi(x))\,dx\geq |U|F(A), \qquad \varphi\in W^{1,\infty}_0(U;\mathbb R^2). \]
The distinction is between testing a single compatible wave and controlling arbitrary combinations of compatible deformations. It is central to the stability of vector-valued variational energies. The planar implication is the relevant form of Morrey’s problem. [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.06367v1)
There is an important current-prior-work boundary. Bruno–Pasqualotto’s 2026 manuscript already establishes the equivalence for rotationally invariant homogeneous quartic polynomials, using heat flow and exact differential-form corrections. I do not count that method or their invariant theorem as an Astra invention. [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06367)
The Burkholder family supplies a more demanding test. Existing positive results include a pointwise distortion restriction in Astala–Iwaniec–Prause–Saksman and, in Guerra’s August 2026 manuscript, restriction to symmetric matrices. Neither restriction is imposed in the obstruction theorem below. [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1012.0504)

\[ E_F(A;B_1,B_2) = D^2F(A)[B_1,B_1]+D^2F(A)[B_2,B_2]. \]

That distinction becomes decisive in the next calculation.
Introduce the complex matrix coordinates
\[ z=\frac{A_{11}+A_{22}}2 +i\frac{A_{21}-A_{12}}2, \qquad w=\frac{A_{11}-A_{22}}2 +i\frac{A_{21}+A_{12}}2. \]
Write
\[ r=|z|,\qquad s=|w|,\qquad R=r+s. \]
For \(p>2\), use the rank-one-convex sign of the Burkholder integrand:
\[ F_p(A)=\big((p-1)s-r\big)R^{p-1}. \tag{4} \]
Work initially on
\[ \mathcal U=\{A:r>0,\ s>0\}. \]
Let
\[ \omega_z=d(\Re z)\wedge d(\Im z),\qquad \omega_w=d(\Re w)\wedge d(\Im w), \]
and define
\[ K_p=2p(p-1)R^{p-2}, \qquad \Omega_p=K_p(\omega_z+\omega_w). \tag{5} \]
At a given matrix, rotate domain and target so that \(z=r\), \(w=s\), and express the compatible jets in those coordinates as in (1).
\[ \boxed{ \begin{aligned} &E_{F_p}(A;B_1,B_2)+\Omega_p(B_1,B_2)\\ &\quad= p(p-2)R^{p-3} \left[ (p-1)s(a^2+b^2) +\frac{R^2}{4r}\big((c-e)^2+(b-d)^2\big) \right]. \end{aligned}} \tag{6} \]
The right-hand side is nonnegative.
At the diagonal representative,
\[ \begin{aligned} 2z_x&=a+e+i(d-b),& 2z_y&=b+f+i(e-c),\\ 2w_x&=a-e+i(d+b),& 2w_y&=b-f+i(e+c). \end{aligned} \]
The radial Hessian coefficients are
\[ \begin{aligned} F_{rr}&=p(p-1)R^{p-3}\big[-r+(p-3)s\big],\\ F_{rs}&=p(p-1)(p-2)sR^{p-3},\\ F_{ss}&=p(p-1)R^{p-3}\big[r+(p-1)s\big], \end{aligned} \]
with angular coefficients
\[ \frac{F_r}{r} =pR^{p-2}\frac{-r+(p-2)s}{r}, \qquad \frac{F_s}{s}=p(p-1)R^{p-2}. \]
Substitution and collection of coefficients gives (6). The supplied symbolic script verifies it with \(p\) left as a parameter.
However,
\[ d\Omega_p=dK_p\wedge(\omega_z+\omega_w)\neq0. \]
It would be incorrect to integrate away this correction using Stokes’ theorem.
The next result shows that a more elaborate closed correction cannot repair this.
For every \(p>2\), there is no \(C^1\) closed two-form \(\omega\) on \(\mathcal U\) satisfying
\[ E_{F_p}(A;B_1,B_2)+\omega_A(B_1,B_2)\geq0 \tag{7} \]
for every \(A\in\mathcal U\) and every compatible pair.
The form need not be polynomial, homogeneous, exact, or bounded near the excluded axes.
Suppose such a certificate exists.
The energy is invariant under independent rotations of \(z,w\), induced by domain and target rotations. Average the certificate over this compact symmetry group. This preserves positivity and closedness.

Before retaining a general quartic heat-flow programme, I tested its simplest hidden assumption.
Take
\[ F(A)=(\det A)^2. \]
This is quasiconvex: the average determinant is fixed by the boundary data, and Jensen’s inequality applies to its square.
Nevertheless, its energy need not decrease under componentwise heat evolution.
On the \(2\pi\)-periodic torus, let
\[ h(x,y)=\sin x+\sin y, \qquad v_0=(h,h^2). \]
Initially,
\[ \det Dv_0=0 \]
everywhere.
The exact heat evolution is
\[ \begin{aligned} v_t^1&=e^{-t}(\sin x+\sin y),\\ v_t^2&= 1-\frac12e^{-4t}(\cos2x+\cos2y) +2e^{-2t}\sin x\sin y. \end{aligned} \]
Its Jacobian is
\[ \det Dv_t = 2e^{-t}(e^{-2t}-e^{-4t}) \cos x\cos y(\sin x-\sin y). \]
Hence, using normalized torus average,
\[ \boxed{ \left\langle(\det Dv_t)^2\right\rangle = \frac12e^{-2t}(e^{-2t}-e^{-4t})^2>0 \qquad(t>0). } \tag{12} \]
The energy rises from zero.
Therefore the statement
Every rank-one-convex planar quartic admits a direct heat-monotonicity proof
is false. A viable operation must at least separate the determinant-square contribution.
The quartic setting has additional structure absent from the nonpolynomial Burkholder family.
For a homogeneous quartic \(F\), symmetry of its four-linear polarization gives
\[ \boxed{ D^2F(A)[H,H]=D^2F(H)[A,A]. } \tag{13} \]
Consequently, if \(F\) is rank-one convex and \(R\) has rank one, then
\[ D^2F(R)[H,H]\geq0 \qquad\text{for every }H. \tag{14} \]
Thus the full Hessian is positive semidefinite at every rank-one matrix.
This yields an exact classification.
